title: Blebitis and Infectious Endophthalmitis: A Comprehensive Clinical Management Protocol
summary: Blebitis represents an ocular emergency characterized by infection of the filtering bleb following trabeculectomy. Without immediate, aggressive intervention, it rapidly progresses to sight-threatening endophthalmitis.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Blebitis is a focal infection involving the filtering bleb post-trabeculectomy. It occurs when pathogens gain entry to the anterior chamber via a compromised bleb wall. Pathogenesis: 1. Bleb avascularity/thinning (leaky bleb). 2. Bacterial colonization (Staphylococcus epidermidis, Streptococcus spp.). 3. Penetration into the bleb and subsequently the vitreous cavity leading to endophthalmitis.

sections.title: Key Risk Factors
content: Inferior limbal site of trabeculectomy
Use of Mitomycin-C (MMC)
Thin, cystic, avascular blebs
Long-term topical antibiotic use
Contact lens wear
Blepharitis or ocular surface disease

rows: Minimal cells, less pain, usually self-limiting
Vitreous involvement, vision loss, severe pain
Anterior chamber cells but no bleb involvement

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Suspect Endophthalmitis
content: Presence of a hypopyon
Vitreous cells or haze on B-scan ultrasound
Significant visual acuity loss (worse than 20/200)
Severe, unrelenting ocular pain
Eyelid edema and chemosis

branches: Stage III: Overt Endophthalmitis (Heavy vitreous debris)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Perform Seidel test to confirm leak site.
Step 2: Slit-lamp examination: Assess bleb density, infiltration, and AC activity.
Step 3: B-scan Ultrasonography to evaluate for vitritis.
Step 4: Aqueous/Vitreous tap (if endophthalmitis is suspected) for culture and sensitivity.
Step 5: Cultures of the conjunctiva and the bleb area (swab).

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: 1. Hospitalization: Mandatory for blebitis/endophthalmitis.
2. Topical Antibiotics: Fortified Vancomycin (50mg/mL) & Fortified Ceftazidime (50mg/mL) every hour.
3. Systemic Coverage: Consider IV Fluoroquinolones (e.g., Moxifloxacin).
4. Cycloplegics: Atropine 1% BID for comfort and synechiae prevention.
5. Intravitreal Injection: If vitritis is present (Vancomycin 1mg/0.1ml + Ceftazidime 2.25mg/0.1ml).
6. Surgical Intervention: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) for dense vitritis.

content.explanation: B: Bacterial culture priority; L: Local antibiotic (fortified); E: Evaluate vitritis; B: Be aggressive with surgery.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Never perform a bleb revision until the active infection is resolved.
Streptococcus species (esp. S. pneumoniae) carry the worst prognosis.
A clear view of the fundus is critical; if lost, treat as endophthalmitis.
Prophylactic antibiotic use post-trabeculectomy is highly controversial.

sections.title: Landmark Considerations
sections.content: Reference the 'Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study' (EVS) for surgical decision-making, acknowledging that bleb-associated endophthalmitis often requires earlier surgical intervention compared to post-cataract cases due to more virulent organisms.
